answer.text: Official answer B; editorial worked explanation: Instantaneous velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time, v=dx/dt, so option B is the definition. Displacement divided by a finite time is average velocity, while distance-based quantities describe speed.
answer.evidence: Official May 2025 Physics HL Paper 1A TZ1 markscheme 2225-6707M, PDF page 3; key and prompt/options individually reconciled with the paired source appearance; editorial explanation independently checked.

answer.text: Official answer B; editorial worked explanation: The object starts from rest, so its speed at 8.0 s is the area under the acceleration-time graph. From 0 to 8.0 s the graph is a triangle of base 8.0 s and height 8.0 m s⁻²: Δv=½(8.0)(8.0)=32 m s⁻¹. Hence option B.

answer.text:
Official answer B checked; editorial worked explanation:

With no air resistance, horizontal velocity remains u cos theta. Returning to the launch height reverses the vertical component while preserving its magnitude, so it is -u sin theta. Therefore B.

Official answer D checked; editorial worked explanation:

The gradient of a displacement-time graph is velocity. Starting from rest requires zero initial gradient; acceleration makes the gradient increase until T, after which constant speed requires a straight line of constant positive gradient. Therefore D.
Official answer C; editorial worked explanation: X and Y are separated by perpendicular radius components R and R, so their straight-line displacement is the chord √(R²+R²)=R√2.
answer.evidence: Official May 2023 Physics HL Paper 1 TZ1 answer grid checked on PDF page 3; worked explanation recalculated from the source.

answer.text: Official answer C; editorial worked explanation: Uniform acceleration gives a=(v₂−v₁)/(t₂−t₁), so III is correct, and v₂²−v₁²=2as, so II is correct. I ignores the nonzero velocity v₁ at X. Thus II and III only.

notes: The least precise relevant measurement limits the justified precision of a calculated result. Keep extra digits during intermediate steps.
